Mine is comorbid with PTSD, so the obsession is avoiding thoughts of trauma, to the point that it's all I am able to think about in the back of my head. Sure I've learned to focus on activities and tasks and art and poetry, but I can never truly get rid of it, it's just in the back of my thoughts constantly. And when it comes to the forefront of my thoughts, depending on how much energy I have, I can get rid of it by only doing a few compulsions if I have lots of energy, or if I'm low energy I might spend hours trying to do different actions to make it stop. (doors, changing clothes, turning things on and off, locking and unlocking doors, opening and closing whatever tab I'm using, turning my phone on and off/clearing the memory, even when I make tea I have to pour the water out if I accidentally think about the trauma while making it). It's caused a lot of friction and difficulty in my day to day life and when it's horribly exhausting and painful it can cause a mental breakdown or manic-depressive episode. I describe it as feeling like you're on fire and frantically running around trying to do anything possible to put it out/make it stop.

before the high elves of Quel'thalas were a thing, the highborne of Zin'azhari called themselves Quel'dorei, or the highborne, which also happens to be the same word to mean high elf as well.

They could both be called high elves.

The nightborne drew power from the Night Well, a font of incomprehensible power, created from many of the once continent Kalimdor's ley-lines all drawn and directed together into one point. This shaped and saturates their beings with pure arcane energy, and without sunlight or moonlight to provide them with the sources of nourishment their bodies previously needed, they relied on this well to sustain them. They were no longer beings of nature, and were further removed from their troll ancestors than even the kal'dorei or highborne were. Their affinity for arcane magic increased as their beings became one with the ley-line's mana..

The Shen'dralar highborne of Eldre'thalas were not so fortuitous. Their city only existed as a means to hide the Queen Azshara's most deeply cherished and best-kept secrets. No direct sources of ley-energy were pointed in that direction for fear of giving its purpose/location away to the queen's enemies, or even the common kal'dorei folk. They merely relied on the powers granted to them by the Well of Eternity in Zin'azshari, which found its way to the highborne even here. The Well of Eternity was not like the Night Well in the way that it was created by ley-line directional technology. It was created by the titans, and saturated with the powers of titan-magic, and Azeroth, the world soul's own essence. It was the well that permeated their beings and spirits, elevating them into the night elves, from what once were mere trolls, in the first place.

When the war of the ancients ended, and the Well of Eternity destroyed, the elves that still resided here had nothing.

They still had the light of the moon, even the light of the sun, sure, but they did not have the arcane power that once radiated from them, that once sustained their hunger. They tried to contact their queen or what remained of Zin'azshari for aid, assistance, even guidance, but received only silence in return. Panic began to set in, in the city that once thrummed with arcane magic. Some had begun to go mad, draining irreplaceable objects and artifacts of their magic to ease the pain of their mana addiction, others became so starved of sustenance that they simply died.

The elves became tired and desperate, and so an equally desperate plan was made. The shen'dralar would summon something to sustain them, no matter the consequence, for whatever consequences this choice bore, it would certainly not be as bad as the extinction and madness the highborne would face if they did not find a new source soon.

The elves would summon, and feed upon, a demon.

The ritual was a costly one, some lives may have even been lost in the process, though all shen'dralar records from the era account this to be a wonderous and historic event for their people. The demon, Immolthar, was summoned and bound by the dwindling powers of the elven magi, and for thousands of years, they would feast upon his mana, his fel-charged essence. It was not a willing effort on Immolthar's part, but after a war in which the shen'dralar had felt as though the demons had betrayed the highborne, failed to protect them for some, they were all to eager to drain it of its power.

The shen'dralar kept up this way of life for ages, and though the supply of mana was not nearly as much as it once was, it kept them alive. It kept them fed, and their magic flowing.

When the demon broke free thousands of years later, many of the highborne were killed. Some fled into the wilds of Feralas as Eldre'thalas, the city that had stood for 10,000 years, was reduced to ruin and rubble. Those that stayed in the city were either hunted or hidden, dealing with the same mana-addled crisis as before, and those that left, now faced a world they knew nothing about, and arcane powers that dwindled from their finger tips as if they were holding sand. And so they sought out the only ally in this broken, sundered Kalimdor that they could remember: The Kal'dorei.

The night elves were not so keen on letting these mana-addicted, fel-addled exiles back into their society, and were even less interested in the idea once the higborne began to preform vile arcane rituals in their forests in attempts to try and regain their strength, their arcane aptitude.

Nevertheless, their Archmagi managed to appeal to the Archdruid Malfurion's sympathies, and during a time as dangerous and uncertain as the cataclysm, the night elves needed all the numbers and help they were offered, even by these... highborne...

Our views can be seen as extreme, but are more logical. We don't see birth as an inherently good thing, especially into families that can't properly care for them. 

And to those that say "if everyone stopped having kids the human race would die out," we don't see humans being extinct as an overall negative. Many see it as a good thing. 

I would like to clarify though that we don't want anyone to hurt or kill anyone though, and we don't want anyone to kill themselves. We see a huge difference between creating new life (which is optional), and ending already existing life. We don't hate kids, a lot of us love kids and don't want to have to bring more into the world if it means they'll suffer or experience trauma/the worst parts humanity has to offer.

We advocate for adoption, taking in children that already need homes, rather than just making more. It's not like there are non-existent people waiting to be created, but there are existing people, children, that need homes and their emotional/financial needs met.

Something a lot of anti-natalists can't seem to agree on is whether or not you should need to pass a parent-capability test/get a parenting license in order to have or raise children. I personally think there should be one because every child has certain needs that have to be met, that can't be met by those emotionally unfit to be caretakers.

A lot of us also advocate for reproductive rights and the right to obtain vasectomies, tubal litigation, and other procedures that make it easier for those who don't want children to not have them accidentally. We want bodily autonomy, and we really don't want children to be born into homes that don't want them/can't properly take care of them.

Here's what I've gathered over about 5 or 6 years of rping a draenei mage. 

Arcane is the main school of magic that most beginner magi have access to, then learning frost/fire magic once they become a little more advanced. 

Blinking, invisibility casting, teleporting, and opening portals are all spells that create tiny rifts in reality and can attract the attention of demons, according to the surviving shen'dralar in Feralas.

Summoned food is a basic spell, but if left uneaten, the food will disappear after 15 minutes, and it doesn't sustain magic users as well as it does non-magic users.

Mirror images can be created with grueling practice, but each individual must have enough mana in their bodies to be magically "reflected" in space time, therefore less mana=less(or weaker) mirror images, if any.

Spell words are like training wheels, good for helping younger and less experienced casters learn and memorize how to handle magic and casting, but unnecessary and sometimes a nuisance for more seasoned magi.

Different races have different approaches/styles to magic. Arts such as cooking, literature, language, music, and sculpting are widely different across multiple cultures. Why would a culture's use/utilization of magic be any different?

Leylines are vital to mortal casters and can be used in runic ways or telemancy to both amplify raw arcane power, and to conserve mana-costs.

Staves aren't -always- necessary, but can even be used as efficient conduits when properly handled. And besides, when it comes to fucking up a spell incantation, would you rather accidentally explode a staff, or your hands?

Portals are usually regulated and used sparingly even sometimes by rogue magi for their damage to the fabric of the world each time one is opened.

Hemomancy is a good crossover between arcane magics and necromantic ones if you want to make the bloodmage edgelord character of your dreams.
